summary: Experiencer coding: Preterit has L-series agents (ḥəlli, ḥəlla, ḥərre); Infectum has its person endings. Targets occur with l-, b-, ʕal-, zero-marked NPs or unintroduced findings. These differences do not establish separate meanings by themselves.
Repeated auditory and olfactory findings support widening I.1: JL 18.7/12; JTM 5.3/33; 63/194,270. Tactile inspection precedes ḥəlli at 63/255. No independent lexical sense “hear” is established.

Infectum-wa covers habitual looking and ongoing inspection. Its actual existing sense-1 count is two: the Russian transfer remark is a note on one example, not an extra example. No structural correction is required in this parsed input.

Discourse Imperativ ḥur before assertions and warnings is already represented by the inherited “Schau, Papa!” example; merge these proposals into I.1. Only the overt controlled preventive dependent clause is introduced as I.4.

Medical inspection in PrS 35/83 is covered by I.1 and parallels the existing doctor example (prs 224/10); sustained care remains I.3. Consulting a divination book is indexed as a collocation, not “open”.

Contractions recur across speakers: ḥōr/ḥor, ḥarno, ḥanno, ḥorno, ḥuyanno and plural ḥərre. Orthographic h/ḥ and ә/ə variation is preserved in decisions but is insufficient alone to justify further full-cell examples.

Routine counts (not individual records): I.1 Preterit 759, Infectum 579, Imperativ 132, Infectum-wa 4; I.3 Infectum 3, Infectum-wa 1; I.2 Infectum-wa 1, Infectum 1. These are supplied aggregate evidence, not additional example texts.

Batch 2 confirms rather than overturns batch 1. Talay 1/50,61 has ḥəlli introducing nonvisual experience while the narrator is blindfolded; 112/274 similarly introduces twittering. These support the broadened I.1 gloss, not an independent lexical “hear” sense.

Forms retaining r: 83/73,75 feminine ḥərla and 84/54 masculine ḥərle. Later masculine-looking ḥəlle with feminine discourse subjects (80/8,89/70) repeats the unresolved agreement/transcription issue from PrS 45/28; no normalization is made.

Attention ḥur occurs with women (78/226,81/91,105) and two wives (97/101). This strengthens the question of an invariant discourse directive but does not prove the answer. It remains sense 1; warnings without a directly governed preventive clause are not automatically I.4.
The cumulative I.1 Imperativ, Infectum and Infectum-wa cells are already adequately represented. Reader thin_cell counts refer to the original entry and were not used to refill them in this batch.

Feminine temporal i ḥyərto d ḥoyər (107/78) parallels i ḥyarto d ḥəlle (65/147), making a recurrent cognate temporal construction likely; verbal Infinitiv versus a lexical glance noun still requires editorial classification.
PrS 9/24: does the edition really read ḥəlle, or xəlle/axəlle? The translation “assen” and meal sequence conflict with the printed looking verb. Withhold the example pending source verification.
PrS 5/22: confirm Ḥəlla after a spoken disclosure. The source supports perception but does not alone prove a lexical hearing sense.
PrS 4/11: is the quotation boundary before Ḥərre displaced, or is the form an unusual Imperativ? PrS 45/28 likewise has masculine-looking Ḥəlle before feminine ḥzela.
JTM 1.3/4 gḥayra: confirm unexpected final -a in the plural context. Lahdo Traitor 2/19 ḥaruwe: confirm the ending and Infectum-wa analysis before adding an example.
Lahdo Traitor 2/13: is ayriwa an actual reduction of ḥayriwa or an omitted initial consonant in transcription?
65/147 ḥyarto and 66/16 ḥyartaṯṯe: productive feminine Infinitiv, a single glance, or lexical “appearance”? Withheld as new Infinitiv examples.
40/27: confirm that the aperture is subject of koḥayro and koʕəbro; the German gives impersonal visual access.
PrS 62/8 Ḥəllili: clarify agent/beneficiary segmentation; do not infer German lassen morphology in Turoyo.

PrS source references are modern text/verse versus inherited edition page/line (PrS 1/29 ~ prs 3/1; 43/52 ~ prs 122/18; 44/75 ~ prs 127/37). Check the reference mapping before replacing legacy citations.
JL 7.7/2: what is the contribution of g- in gḥayriwayna after naqqa? JL 17.6/7: confirm ṇ transcription and contraction in gḥaṇṇo.
MAC NE Shangali Pangali/16 and PrS 40/75: is short ḥur usable independently of addressee gender/number, or is this local address/transcription?
107/39 has an alignment flag: the German omits “three nights” in the Turoyo three-days-and-three-nights custom. No example or translation is quoted from that flagged occurrence.
96/251 kḥotər in kḥoyər w lo kḥotər: confirm the likely y/t transcription or printing error against the edition; no novel form is published.
97/156: confirm the contextual interpretation of l baxte as conscience/honour rather than a different reading of baxt. The collocation is supported by one attestation.
80/8 and 89/70: check masculine-looking ḥəlle with feminine actors, alongside the earlier PrS 45/28 case; 83/73,75 provides clear contrasting feminine ḥərla.

Animal subjects (horse, young storks) and the eye as subject retain ordinary perception. Bare NPs and following clauses supplement the listed prepositional targets; do not rewrite inherited government solely for formatting.
Architectural subjects express orientation, with l-, ʕal- or a viewing scope. Human subjects looking out through a window/tent share the existing spatial sense.
Care extends to churches, monasteries, schools and goats; l-, b- and ʕal- occur. Administrative supervision is a participant extension, not a separate numbered sense.
